articles.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
articles.snippet: The unprecedented International Court of Justice verdict concerns a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands.
articles.full_text:
Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
- Published
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
'Recognition of our suffering'
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.
Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attachÃ© be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.
He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

articles.title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
articles.snippet: While the presidents have previously met for one-on-one meetings, this is their first trilateral discussion.
articles.full_text:
Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
- Published
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.
In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.
Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".
Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.
In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.
While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".
He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".
Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.
This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
- Published14 hours ago
The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.
Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".
Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.
China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."
Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".
It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."
"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".
Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.
He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".
Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".
He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.
As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.
Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.
In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.
There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.
The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.
"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.
"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."
The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.
"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."
Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.
It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".
Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.
Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.
The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.
US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries.
"I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends".
"We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added.
"Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."
Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment.
"President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.
With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon

articles.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
articles.snippet: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
articles.full_text:
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
- Published
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
US President Donald Trump's envoys were also there, and his son-in-law Jared Kushner said Trump wanted to make a deal with Russia "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition. Russia has never accepted the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but Article Five-style guarantees could theoretically be offered to Kyiv without being part of the Western defensive alliance.
Zelensky and the three European leaders - Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron - were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials haven't budged from Russia's demands for Ukraine sovereign territory.
As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And today, Putin vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready for making compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.
"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said.

articles.title: Dozens missing after boat carrying migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
articles.snippet: At least four bodies have been recovered from the boat which was reportedly carrying between 50 and 100 people.
articles.full_text:
Dozens missing after boat carrying migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
- Published
Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat said to be carrying between 50 and 100 migrants capsized in the Atlantic Ocean.
Four bodies have reportedly been recovered so far. Dozens of people are still missing.
Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.
This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).
"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.
A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.
However, a local official told Reuters news agency it was carrying 50 people, adding that the boat hit a rock as migrants were transferring from small fishing boats to a larger vessel.
Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.
He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.
Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.
Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.
The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.
It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.
The Senegalese navy said it had rescued more than 1,400 people on Monday and Tuesday this week.
As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.
They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.
They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.
On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.
It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

articles.title: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
articles.snippet: The bridge - a symbol of Russia's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula - suffered major damaged following a combined attack by Ukraine earlier this week.
articles.full_text:
Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
- Published
Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.
In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.
A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.
But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.
Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.
Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles.
From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplied its troops in southern Ukraine.
Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."
The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.
The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.
It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.
Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.
Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.
In response to Tuesday's hit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But the operation to repair it could take a long time, and it will likely have to be carried out under frequent Ukrainian fire.
Russia has regularly targeted Ukrainian civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
This week alone, as the Crimean Bridge was being hit, Moscow targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

articles.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
articles.snippet: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Vincent van Gogh's life.
articles.full_text:
Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
- Published
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (Â£144.8m).
The sale of ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.
The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.
The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (Â£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.
Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.
Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.
A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.
"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.
Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.
It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it in 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.
The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.
Four other owners then had the painting.
The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

articles.title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's removal
articles.snippet: The US Secretary of Defence says Venezuela has "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner".
articles.full_text:
Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's removal
- Published
The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, NicolÃ¡s Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.
The interim government led by Delcy RodrÃguez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.
Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months.
Interim President RodrÃguez said the deal would help confront "common threats".
Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo ChÃ¡vez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.
ChÃ¡vez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government.
He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government".
Under NicolÃ¡s Maduro, who succeeded ChÃ¡vez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.
They reached rock bottom late last year when the US doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro's capture to $50m (Â£38m) and eventually seized him on 3 January in a military raid.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now in custody in New York on charges of drug-trafficking and conspiracy to commit torture, which they deny.
Hegseth addressed the change in the two countries' relationship since Maduro was seized in his speech at the US embassy in Caracas on Wednesday.
"It's a great honour to be here as the first United States Secretary of War this century to set foot in Venezuela. The weight of this moment does not escape me," he said.
"Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable," he added before recalling a public appearance by then-President Maduro which had angered the Trump administration.
"Exactly one year ago today, the indicted narco-terrorist fugitive NicolÃ¡s Maduro, the man who spent more than a decade handing Venezuela's borders and territory to terrorists from all over the world, stood on a stage, not too far from here, and yelled mockingly: 'Come and get me!'. Well, we answered that call."
Hegseth added that the result of the US military raid on 3 January had been as Maduro predicted, quoting the deposed leader's words: "No war, yes peace."
He described the deal signed by him and Venezuela's defence minister on Wednesday as a "new chapter for the United States, for Venezuela, for the Venezuelan military and for the Western Hemisphere through the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition".
RodrÃguez described it as "extraordinarily relevant for our bilateral relations".
"In a matter of months, secretary, we have turned very difficult moments for our people into a space for co-operation and mutual benefit for both of our countries," she said addressing Hegseth during a meeting at the presidential palace.
While no details of the deal have been published, in her speech RodrÃguez mentioned the training of Venezuela's armed forces and improving its "operational equipment" and access to new technology "to confront shared threats".
In his speech at the US embassy, Hegseth was more direct about who he considers to be those threats. Addressing "the narco-terrorists who abuse this [Venezuela] as a safe haven", he warned that "we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you".
From Venezuela, Hegseth travelled on to neighbouring Colombia, whose president, Abelardo de la Espriella, is a close ally of the Trump administration.
Colombia is already part of the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition and in August, Hegseth had floated the possibility of joint US-Colombian military operations against armed groups.
On Wednesday, President de la Espriella took to X to deny a report by the New York Times which had stated that he had rejected carrying out joint operations, external.
In his post, he stressed that any decision would be taken while respecting Colombia's constitution, and the country's laws and sovereignty.
Hegseth reposted the tweet commenting that the US-Colombian partnership "is stronger than ever before".

articles.title: Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her two sons
articles.snippet: At a hearing on the possibility of parole, Smith said she wished she could change the past, and her two children "did not deserve to die".
articles.full_text:
Susan Smith denied parole again 32 years after drowning her two sons
- Published
A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago has been denied parole for a second time.
Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and rolling her vehicle into a lake in 1994.
"I got to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake," Smith said during a hearing on Thursday with the state board that decides whether to release those in prison on parole.
The seven-member board later unanimously turned down her request to be freed. The father of the two boys has vowed to continue to oppose her release, and several people spoke against her in the hearing.
Smith, whose lawyers had argued she suffered a mental breakdown during the crime, can apply to the South Carolina Board of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services for parole every two years.
She told the board that she had changed and matured since killing three-year-old Michael and one-year-old Alex, and that "I am not the same person I was 32 years ago".
She also said she was "very, very sorry" and that she would go back and change the circumstances if she could.
"They were innocent children," Smith said. "They did not deserve to die."
Her children's father, David Smith, attended the hearing so he could advocate for their sons, he said.
The 32 years, he said, do not take away what Smith "deliberately" did.
"I know in my heart granting her parole would be a huge injustice to Michael and Alex," said David Smith, who had pinned a photo of both his sons to his lapel.
Prosecutors argued during the trial that Smith killed the boys after a man with whom she was having an affair told her that her sons were the reason that the pair did not have a future together.
At Thursday's hearing, Smith said: "This did not happen because of a man. That's just not true."
When the boys first disappeared, Smith said she was carjacked late at night and a man drove away with her car. While she pleaded publicly for their safe return, her sons were at the bottom of a nearby lake.
But ultimately she confessed to the crime.
Defence lawyers said she had wanted to die with her children but left the car at the last minute.
Smith was convicted of murder. Under South Carolina law at the time, she was allowed to request parole every two years after serving 30 years in prison.
In the US, some people convicted of crimes are eligible for parole, which means they can be released from incarceration.
She would have needed two-thirds of the board members present to vote in her favour to be freed.

articles.title: France awaits verdict six years after police beat Black music producer
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Three officers are accused of assaulting Michel Zecler in an incident that was filmed by surveillance cameras.
articles.full_text:
France awaits verdict six years after police beat Black music producer
Three officers are accused of assaulting Michel Zecler in an incident that was filmed by surveillance cameras.
Paris, France – Six years ago, Michel Zecler was assaulted by the three officers at his Parisian music studio.
Surveillance camera footage shows the officers pushing Zecler, who is Black, inside his studio and beating him until other musicians intervened on November 21, 2020.
Aurelien Lapersonne, Pierre Plantier and Philippe Tondeux are accused of striking the music producer 29 times in four minutes, and an additional six times in the face after Zecler was already handcuffed.
The verdict is expected on Friday.
The case fuelled wider concerns in France about police brutality and caught the public’s attention. At the time, football star Kylian Mbappe shared an image of a heavily injured Zecler, blood running from his face, with the words: “Unbearable video. Unacceptable violence”.
The three French police officers are also accused of forging a public document.
During the attack, the officers allegedly made multiple racist remarks towards Zecler. All three signed a falsified police report stating that Zecler hit the police officers – a claim refuted by surveillance footage.
“It’s pretty obvious that this case is about institutional racism, systemic discrimination and police violence. Everything is connected. Not only are we dealing with police violence against a Black man, but that’s on top of attempting to conceal evidence and falsify a report,” Rim-Sarah Alouane, a legal scholar and an associate researcher in public law at the University of Toulouse Capitole, told Al Jazeera. “When these reports are falsified, we’re questioning the integrity of the entire system.”
The prosecution’s office requested a permanent ban on all three officers, along with prison sentences.
The prosecutor called for a jail sentence of six years without parole for Lapersonne, the officer who initiated the police identity check and submitted the falsified report, a five-year sentence for the trio’s leader, Tondeux, the most experienced officer present, and four years for the third police officer, Plantier.
“There is no room for a symbolic sentence,” a representative of the public prosecutor’s office said in a statement. “We are talking about crimes, violence and racial slurs. About a complete lack of control over what was done and an absolute determination to get away with it in the end.”
‘If there was no footage, we would not be here today’
A series of court cases has identified the systemic discrimination among the police in France.
Last year, the European Court of Human Rights condemned France for racial profiling of Karim Touil, a young French national of North African origin who was stopped by police three times within 10 days in November and December 2011.
In October 2023, France’s high court acknowledged racial profiling during police identity checks but did not require French authorities to take the “necessary measures to end this longstanding, abusive practice”, Human Rights Watch (HRW) noted.
In 2021, the French government was condemned for “gross negligence” in an identity check of three high school students in at Gare du Nord in Paris.
Although concerns about police violence in France are not new, this trial is pivotal because of the surveillance footage and attempted cover-up, Alouane noted.
“This trial brings to light those issues that human rights organisations have been documenting for years. It gives an illustration, through a proper case, about the use of force and systemic violence that we’ve known about for years,” Alouane said. “If there was no footage, we would not be here today. The police would have gotten away with it.”
Police officer Lapersonne, who submitted the report, initially claimed that Zecler attacked the officers and “struck out with his arms and legs”. When the presiding judge asked if he had “made that up”, Lapersonne responded, “Absolutely.” Lapersonne’s initial police report also failed to mention that the officers landed blows on Zecler.
“I deliberately omitted them. I think out of fear. It was stupid of me,” Lapersonne told the presiding judge.
For Alouane, this case revealed the tactics behind systemic police violence in France.
“The falsified documents aspect is crucial to illustrate why this case advanced and the public attention it received. In this case, the footage directly contradicted the police’s claims. The cops knew they did something wrong,” she said. “This is a serious accusation and not an isolated incident.”
The trial comes as France’s Senate considers a controversial bill that would presume police officers and gendarmes acted in self-defence when using firearms in the line of duty, which would place the burden of proof on the complainant. Critics call the proposal a “licence to kill”. The National Assembly approved the measure in July.
“It’s a very dangerous piece of legislation. It’s liberticide. It would create a sense of impunity amongst police officers — which already exists, but this would strengthen that. It would undermine investigations and make access to the justice system even more difficult for victims and their families,” Alouane said. “It raises serious issues regarding equality under the law because it puts a presumption of innocence in favour of people because of their profession as cops.”
Legislation like the self-defence law could inhibit cases like Zecler’s in the future, Alouane noted.
“If this proposal were in place, we would not have this case. It would have been dismissed today,” she said.
French police are also under scrutiny for their tactics during recent student protests. A 15-year-old lost a hand from a police stun grenade, and another officer threw a tear gas canister at close range, shattering a 14-year-old’s jaw and several teeth.

Palestinians in Gaza face new displacement after Israeli army operation
Families in Nuseirat spend the night without shelter, while many fear returning despite Israel announcing the end of its raid.
Nuseirat, Gaza Strip – For the 13th time, Suhail al-Mashharawi has been forced to flee. The 50-year-old Palestinian and his family of eight spent the night in a schoolyard in central Gaza, without blankets, bedding or enough clothing to protect his children from the cold.
Thousands of Palestinians have once again been forced to abandon their makeshift shelters as Israeli forces launched a major ground operation in the enclave, the first major offensive publicly announced by the military since a ceasefire was agreed in October 2025.

On Wednesday, the Israeli military issued forced evacuation orders covering three blocks north of the Nuseirat refugee camp, saying its troops were targeting a suspected Hamas tunnel.
The military announced on Thursday that it had completed its operation and reopened Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south thoroughfare.
While some Palestinians began returning to check on their belongings, others stayed away, saying that sporadic gunfire continued and the road remained unsafe.
For al-Mashharawi, the operation ended a year of relative stability, forcing him and his family to abandon their tent and seek refuge at a nearby educational centre.
He described the conditions there as “dire”, saying his family had received no humanitarian assistance and had no idea how long they would have to stay.
‘Fleeing death into the unknown’
About 6,000 Palestinians fled the area on Wednesday, Gaza’s Government Media Office said.
Israel said the operation targeted a tunnel that threatened its troops. Hamas condemned the incursion as a violation of the ceasefire, while the Israeli military accused the group of violating the agreement.
More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health authorities.
About 1.4 million Palestinians across Gaza now live in tents or makeshift shelters, according to United Nations humanitarian figures.
Ismail Younis, who manages a camp for displaced people in the al-Mufti area, said bullets penetrated the tents during the operation, with a quadcopter flying over the camp, prompting families to flee quickly.
“The families left without having a specific destination, or an alternative place for them to take refuge,” he said. “Their main concern was to save their lives and the lives of their children, in light of the escalating gunfire and continued shelling.”
Amna al-Qassas, 49, was one of those who had to rapidly flee her camp in Nuseirat when the forced evacuation came. She had time to pack only a small bag containing her family’s identification documents.
Al-Qassas fled with 10 family members, leaving behind the tent and possessions she had managed to salvage during an earlier displacement from the Tuffah neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City.
She told Al Jazeera that displacement had become a “recurring nightmare”, taking her family back to square one and destroying what little sense of security they had regained.
Now, they were being forced to leave again. “We have not had time to think … our only concern was to escape death, even if it meant fleeing into the unknown,” she said.
Unable to find a vehicle to transport her belongings, al-Qassas left everything behind. She fears the destruction of her shelter could leave her with nothing to return to.

articles.title: ‘Not an acquittal’: After impeachment vote, Hegseth still under microscope
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: A week after a fizzled impeachment bid, analysts say Hegseth continues to face backlash for his leadership at Pentagon.
articles.full_text:
‘Not an acquittal’: After impeachment vote, Hegseth still under microscope
A week after a fizzled impeachment bid, analysts say Hegseth continues to face backlash for his leadership at Pentagon.
In the wake of the United States midterm elections, attention has turned to whether Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will be able to preserve his cabinet-level position once Congress’s new Democratic majorities are sworn in.
Already, the Fox News host-turned-military-chief has faced mounting calls for his removal from office.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Did Democrats save Hegseth from impeachment?
- list 2 of 4Trump’s White House calls Democratic plans for congressional probes ‘abuse’
- list 3 of 4How does Iran view Trump sidelining Vance from talks?
- list 4 of 4US Navy chief says Iran war has put ‘strain’ on maritime forces
But analysts question the extent to which Hegseth’s impeachment would affect military policy under President Donald Trump.
“Ultimately, the secretary of defence is a powerful participant in shaping a war,” said Jasmine El-Gamal, a former Middle East adviser in the Pentagon.
El-Gamal, however, believes targeting Hegseth alone would not be enough to secure accountability for decisions like launching the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hegseth holds significant power in directing the US war effort, she explained, but he also works hand-in-hand with the president and his advisers.
“Calling him merely an ‘executor’ understates that power, while calling him its sole architect understates the president’s power and obscures where particular decisions were actually made,” El-Gamal said.
Facing impeachment
Since he was sworn in on January 25, 2025, Hegseth has overseen some of Trump’s most controversial international campaigns, including the war on Iran and a series of deadly boat strikes in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean.
Both campaigns have been accused of violating international law. The Iran war, in particular, became a political albatross for Trump’s Republican Party during the midterm race.
A poll earlier this month found that 44 percent of US voters said they were less likely to vote for a midterm candidate who supported the war.
That number dwarfed the 13 percent who said they were more inclined to vote for such a candidate, by a ratio of more than three to one.
The Democratic Party scored a thumping victory in the November 3 midterms, flipping both the House of Representatives and the Senate from Republican control.
Less than a week later, Hegseth faced a push for impeachment, led by outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie.
Among the eight articles of impeachment Massie filed were accusations that Hegseth had dismantled fundamental safeguards to protect civilian lives, leading to incidents like the bombing of an elementary school in Minab, Iran, that killed at least 120 children.
But the impeachment proceedings were shelved on November 10, after the Republicans’ lame-duck majority in the House voted 211 to 204 to block the measure. Eleven Democrats were absent for the vote.
Scrutiny of Pentagon chiefs
Hegseth is hardly the first Pentagon chief to face pressure to leave office following a dismal election for his party.
In November 2006, Republicans likewise suffered a midterm rout amid a groundswell of voter ire over the US-led wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Both chambers of Congress that year flipped to Democratic control.
Within a day of the vote, then-President George W Bush announced that his defence secretary, the late Donald Rumsfeld, would resign. He cited the Iraq war in his remarks.
“I recognise that many Americans voted last night to register their displeasure with the lack of progress being made there,” Bush said of the conflict.
Hegseth, however, has resisted calls for his resignation. In a five-minute video posted two days after the midterms, Hegseth dismissed his critics as “deep-state radicals” obsessed with “political theatre”.
“They attack us because we are effective. It’s not going to work. We will not back down,” Hegseth said. “We put America and the war-fighter first, always and without apology. And that fight continues in the lame-duck Congress.”
His message of defiance included an appeal for the military to “stay the course”, including in the war against Iran.
“I’ll assure you, we have only just begun to fight,” Hegseth added. “We are more determined than ever, more resolute than ever to finish what we have started.”
A key role in the war
Some of the criticism, however, has come from within Hegseth’s own party. Vice President JD Vance, for instance, said the “real reason” the Republicans lost the midterms is “obvious to almost everyone”.
“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote on social media.
Hala Rharrit, a former US diplomat who spent 18 years in the State Department, was among the officials who resigned before Trump took office for his second term, in protest of the US involvement in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
She explained that Hegseth would have been critical in guiding some of the Iran war’s most divisive moments.
The bombing of the Minab elementary school, for example, took place on February 28, the first day of the conflict.
Rharrit said Hegseth and other senior Department of Defense (DOD) officials would have drawn up the initial strike lists before advising Trump on the targets for final approval.
“I suspect that Trump would not get into the granularities of which targets to strike on day one,” Rharrit told Al Jazeera.
“Hegseth and others in DOD had a lot to do with those precise decisions, which also runs through lawyers.”
She also drew a line between decisions taken by Hegseth and Trump and the losses the US and its allies have endured since the war began.
Iran has retaliated against US and Israeli attacks with strikes across the Middle East. At least 23 US service members have died in the conflict, and 865 were wounded.
“Ultimately, they are both responsible, not just for the strikes in Iran, but also for making American service members and diplomats throughout the region sitting ducks,” said Rharrit.
Congress reasserting its authority?
Throughout the war, Congress has had the power to pull the emergency cord and stop the fighting, according to Brian Finucane, who served as a legal adviser in the State Department from 2011 to 2021.
Under the Constitution, “the overwhelming bulk of war powers belong” to the members of Congress, he said.
He sees the midterm results, in part, as a backlash to the Trump administration’s expansive use of executive power.
After all, critics say officials like Hegseth have offered Congress relatively little transparency in the military’s overseas actions.
“We’ve seen sort of the apex of presidential unilateralism under Trump,” Finucane said. “I think it has reminded Americans of why the Constitution gives Congress, not one man, the power to take the country to war.”
The incoming Democrat-led Congress has pledged to use its power to check Trump’s war-making powers and confront Hegseth over his policies.
In the final days of the midterm race, Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, who is now in line to become the first Black speaker of the House, told supporters that Hegseth’s days were numbered.
“In the majority, one of the first things we’re going to do is run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Jeffries said.
He has since described himself as a “hard yes” on impeachment proceedings against the Pentagon chief.
But El-Gamal cautioned against treating the impeachment vote as the only path to accountability.
“Impeachment is just one constitutional accountability mechanism,” said El-Gamal.
She pointed to congressional investigations and the legislature’s “power of the purse” — its authority over federal spending — as two other avenues for reining in Hegseth and Trump.
El-Gamal added that November’s blocked impeachment motion “was not an acquittal nor a vote resolving the allegations” of war crimes in Iran and elsewhere. She anticipates the new Congress, once sworn in, will continue to pursue those allegations.

articles.title: Pentagon lacks ‘overarching plan’ for munitions production, watchdog warns
articles.snippet: “DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study.
articles.full_text:
Facing depleted stockpiles, the Pentagon is briskly trying to ramp up manufacturing of munitions.
The problem is that it is ordering missiles, artillery shells and other munitions without regard to what the military actually needs, according to a new report.
“DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study.
Pentagon officials told investigators that “in lieu of a plan, DoD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.”
The GAO report is the public version of a classified study completed in September 2026. Thus, it doesn’t include “information that DOD deemed classified or sensitive, such as trends in DoD munitions inventories, persistent shortfalls and how these shortfalls have affected DOD’s support to war plans.”
Nonetheless, the report does hint at a mismatch — real and potential — between what the Pentagon is buying and what the military needs.
The Army is desperately trying to boost production of 155mm howitzer shells after
shortages were exacerbated in support of allies and partners. That effort is already plagued by manufacturing woes such as a new Texas plant that cost nearly $500 million, but failed to produce any shell components.
Now the question is exactly how many shells the Army needs.
The “Army’s ramp-up in production of 155-millimeter artillery shells to address shortages exacerbated by U.S. support to allies and partners was not driven by a need to address DoD’s total munitions requirement,” GAO said.
Nor does the Pentagon have a good grasp on how much ammunition it actually has.
Each military service has its data system to track munitions inventories, which is then aggregated by DoD’s Munitions Readiness Initiative to provide, in theory, a near real-time glimpse of stockpiles as well as supply chain links.
“In total, MRI pulls from 37 DOD data sources through a mix of automated connections and some manually updated data,” GAO noted.
However, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment “does not consistently reconcile MRI munitions inventory data against the services’ own data systems.” Nor does it have “a data management plan detailing how data is aggregated in the MRI tool from across the services.”
Authority over munitions inventories is also fragmented among multiple offices within the DoD and the program executive offices in individual services. Working groups that are supposed to bring them together lack authority and accountability.
All of which points to the root of the problem: no one is really in charge. “DoD has not identified an office or entity and delegated to it authority that empowers the leadership to make decisions that improve munitions inventories departmentwide and hold them accountable for the outcomes achieved, such as improving munitions inventory levels,” the GAO report notes.
GAO recommended that DoD create an overarching plan to match munitions requirements, production and funding, as well as metrics to track progress. Without it, the report warns, the “DoD and the services are not well-positioned to address persistently low munitions inventories or risk, for example, investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement.”

articles.title: France and Sweden hold first joint nuclear-deterrence exercise
articles.snippet: The exercise didn’t involve actual nuclear weapons and was not directed at any country, the defense ministries said.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — France and Sweden held their first joint exercise under the forward deterrence initiative proposed by French President Emmanuel Macron, with French nuclear-capable Rafale jets and an Airbus A330 MRTT tanker aircraft operating over Sweden alongside Swedish Gripen fighters.
The exercise, dubbed Excalibur, was held in northern Sweden on Nov. 16 to 18, with the aim of improving interoperability between the French and Swedish air forces, the two countries’ armed forces said in statements on Thursday. The exercise didn’t involve actual nuclear weapons and was not directed at any country, the defense ministries said.
The French-Swedish cooperation follows an exercise last month in which British Eurofighter Typhoon jets escorted French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission. France has been working with several European allies to implement Macron’s proposal to bolster European deterrence, in the face of nuclear saber-rattling by Russia and uncertainty about United States security guarantees.
France’s nuclear deterrent consists of an ocean-based component comprising strategic ballistic-missile submarines, as well as an airborne component consisting of Rafale jets capable of carrying nuclear-tipped cruise missiles developed by MBDA.
“Since the in-depth dialogue on ‘forward deterrence’ was initiated, France and Sweden are taking steps to implement their common roadmap for strategic cooperation,” the Swedish Armed Forces said. The exercise “demonstrates our joint readiness and capability to act together and reflects the commitment of our two countries towards deterring threats and strengthening allied security.”
The deployment of the Rafale jets alongside Gripen fighters, with the support of an A330 MRTT, demonstrated the high level of interoperability between the two air forces in the areas of nuclear deterrence, in the service of Europe’s security, the French Armed Forces General Staff said in a post on the social network X.
“This type of deployment not only allows to test the dispersion of French aircraft to improve their capability to survive an adversary disabling strike, but also opens the door for new modes of operation previously unimaginable, such as attacking targets deep within the Russian Arctic or planning much smaller raids without needing in-flight refueling,” said Etienne Marcuz, a senior analyst at the Fondation pour la Recherche Stratégique, in a post on X.
Sweden’s Gripen fighters are “excellent combat aircraft” specifically designed to penetrate Russian ground-to-air and air-to-air defense systems, and they could be valuable assets during a nuclear strike mission, while freeing up conventional Rafale jets for other missions, Marcuz said.

articles.title: F-35C completes first launch and recovery trials on a Ford-class carrier
articles.snippet: Two Navy F-35C Lightning II fighters have completed the jet’s first round of launch and recovery testing aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy.
articles.full_text:
Two Navy F-35C Lightning II fighters have completed the jet’s first round of launch and recovery testing aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy, the Navy’s second Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier, Lockheed Martin said Thursday.
Over 11 days of testing that began Oct. 13, the Navy’s 251st birthday, the two jets made 34 flights and logged 122 catapult launches and 122 arrested landings, the company said. The aircraft belong to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23, or VX-23, known as the “Salty Dogs,” at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland.
The flights were part of Kennedy’s Aircraft Compatibility Testing, which assesses how the ship’s launch and recovery equipment works with Navy aircraft, according to the Navy. The first arrested landing came on Oct. 13, and the first catapult launch on Oct. 14, Navy photo captions show.
Unlike Nimitz-class carriers, which launch and recover aircraft with steam catapults and hydraulic arresting gear, Ford-class carriers use the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System, or EMALS, and the Advanced Arresting Gear, or AAG. Lockheed said EMALS allows smoother, more precisely controlled launches, while AAG can handle a broader range of recovery conditions.
The Ford class also has a smaller island, the tower that houses the bridge and flight control, set about 140 feet farther back than on Nimitz-class ships. Lockheed said the island and a redesigned flight deck change airflow, exhaust patterns and deck operations.
The at-sea testing followed shore-based trials conducted from January 2024 to May 2025, the company said. It validated the jet’s structural models and verified the software and equipment behind EMALS and AAG. The data will help develop the launch and recovery guidance crews use on Ford-class ships.
“This is a critical event for the F-35C, Kennedy, and the United States Navy,” said Sean Jackson, vice president of Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Development Program. “For the first time, the aircraft has demonstrated launch and recovery operations from a Gerald R. Ford-Class flight deck, advancing the integration of fifth-generation fighter capability with the world’s most advanced carrier technology.”
Jackson also said that upon completion of this test phase, “the Navy has now cleared the F-35C for operations across its entire fleet of aircraft carriers.”
“The ships are cleared to launch and recover F-35s once the launch and recovery bulletins are published,” a Lockheed official told Defense News. “They will not be ready to deploy until fully outfitted with supporting equipment.”
The Navy, the official added, has the “final clearance.”
The F-35C first landed on a carrier in November 2014, aboard USS Nimitz off San Diego, and has since deployed from modified Nimitz-class carriers. The lead ship of the Ford class, USS Gerald R. Ford, has not deployed with the jet.
In 2019, a Navy spokesman told USNI News that both carrier classes could operate with F-35Cs by design but needed changes, such as more robust jet blast deflectors and classified spaces, for the jet to be more effective on a full-length deployment. Stars and Stripes reported in October that the Navy plans to retrofit the Ford to operate the F-35C.
Kennedy received those modifications during construction. In 2020, the Navy changed the ship’s construction contract to meet a legislative requirement that Kennedy be capable of deploying with the F-35C.
The Navy took preliminary acceptance of Kennedy on Sept. 29, after the ship completed acceptance trials in August. Preliminary acceptance allows the crew to test and train at sea while the shipbuilder finishes its work. The Navy said at the time that the ship was about 99% complete, and formal delivery is planned for spring 2027.

articles.snippet: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new agreement on military cooperation with Venezuela in his first visit to the country since U.S. special forces deposed President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid.
articles.full_text:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new agreement on military cooperation with Venezuela on Wednesday as he made his first visit to the country since U.S. special forces deposed President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid in Caracas.
Hegseth announced the agreement alongside Venezuelan acting President Delcy Rodriguez, who welcomed him to the presidential palace. He said it covered joint training, intelligence sharing and other aspects of U.S.-Venezuelan military cooperation. Rodriguez said the arrangement would help confront “common threats” and strengthen training for Venezuela’s armed forces.
Hegseth said the partnership would herald a significant ramp-up in joint action against drug trafficking groups.
“To the narco terrorists who have used this as a safe haven, your time is up. We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you,” Hegseth said, speaking from the U.S. embassy.
Washington already holds growing influence in Venezuela, particularly in the oil sector. Since Maduro’s removal, U.S. officials have moved quickly to shape the country’s future, focusing on energy policy and investment.
That role expanded sharply in August under a deal granting producer North American Blue Energy Partners, or NABEP, long-term access to 17 oilfields that contain about a fifth of the country’s oil reserves through a partnership with the U.S. government. The United States secured a 35% stake in NABEP’s parent, a guaranteed share of output and first refusal rights on the remainder.
NABEP plans oil outpost boost
Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan businessman who controls NABEP and was central to the agreement, told reporters he discussed the progress of oil cooperation with Hegseth, adding that NABEP plans to produce over 250,000 barrels per day of oil by year-end as it prepares to have 10 well clusters in service. That would be an increase from the 224,000 bpd it produced in mid-October, according to company figures.
Hegseth’s trip to Venezuela came two weeks after voter anger over the Iran war helped drive an election defeat for President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in Congress. The unpopular, nearly nine-month-old conflict has driven up gasoline prices in the U.S. and around the world, as Iran fires on tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz off its coast.
Hegseth, who has defended the Iran war as courageous, said the oil deal with Venezuela “makes the Strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the Western Hemisphere.”
Columbia security cooperation
Hegseth’s Caracas stop came at the start of a trip to Latin America. Later on Wednesday, he flew to Colombia to deliver military equipment and discuss security cooperation with Bogota.
Colombia’s defense minister said Hegseth was due to hand over a Lockheed Martin Hercules C-130 aircraft and discuss U.S. support as Colombia battles drug trafficking groups and other illegal armed actors.
In August, Hegseth floated the possibility of joint strikes on Colombian armed groups. The New York Times, however, reported on Wednesday that Colombia’s new right-wing President Abelardo De La Espriella rejected that plan because of a lack of votes in Congress.
A U.S. official, speaking to Reuters on condition of anonymity, confirmed concerns in Bogota about support in Congress. But the official did not say De La Espriella had rejected the plan outright.
Colombia’s defense and foreign ministries referred questions to the president’s office, which did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Speaking alongside Hegseth, Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula said any decision by the executive branch in such circumstances would require congressional approval, adding that the government was confident it would secure lawmakers’ backing. “We cannot afford to waste time in the fight against crime,” he said.
Bula also said De La Espriella had been clear about Colombia’s sovereign position and that Hegseth understood the country’s democratic institutions and internal decision-making processes.
Later on Wednesday, De La Espriella denied the New York Times report, saying he had not rejected any proposal from Trump’s administration and that Colombia’s cooperation with the United States focused on strengthening its security forces rather than seeking foreign troops. He added that any deployment of foreign forces would require congressional approval.
The comments come as the Colombian Congress debates a tax reform bill that De La Espriella’s government has struggled to advance, prompting the administration to soften the proposal to help secure its passage.
Trump’s Latin America policy has expanded dramatically beyond its early focus on the Panama Canal. U.S. military strikes on suspected drug boats have killed more than 200 people since they began last year.
As he addressed a gathering at the embassy, Hegseth invoked a revamped Monroe Doctrine, the 19th-century policy asserting U.S. primacy across the Americas that critics associate with decades of U.S. intervention.
He called it the “Donroe Doctrine” — a play on Trump’s name.
“That is the Donroe Doctrine. Venezuela has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner on its way to rebuilding its military alongside the United States,” Hegseth said.

articles.title: Ukraine plans to double drone supplies, triple deep strikes
articles.snippet: Ukraine is forging ahead with its long-range strike campaign with support from European partners, despite Washington’s request to prioritize front-line defense and associated midrange strikes instead.
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine plans to double its drone supplies and more than triple its long-range strike capabilities next year, according to Ukraine’s defense minister, as Kyiv presses ahead with its long-range strike campaign despite the Pentagon’s criticism of attacks deep inside Russia.
Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara made the announcements Tuesday at a press conference after the 37th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
“There are prospects in this, and we are only getting started,” he said.
A day later, the British government said in a statement that it will send Ukraine more than 1,000 long-range strike drones, some able to fly more than 620 miles (1,000 kilometers), in a roughly $342 million (£260 million) package.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to announce the offer Thursday in Berlin at a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing” of Ukraine supporters, where U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steven Witkoff are expected to brief European leaders on peace negotiations.
Ukraine is forging ahead with its long-range strike campaign with support from European partners, despite Washington’s request to prioritize front-line defense and associated midrange strikes instead.
Khmara told the EU Foreign Affairs Council that drones will make up more than half of Ukraine’s weapons needs in 2027. At the press conference, he said 62% of funding should go to drones, including first-person-view, middle-strike, deep-strike and logistics drones.
“While the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line,” Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby said in his opening remarks to the meeting.
Such strikes, “especially those that target civilian infrastructure, such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate,” he said.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius responded in a press conference after the meeting, stating that faulting strikes on “strategic military and military use targets” in Russia is “quite a stupid thing, I think.”
“We should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on civil energy, water and heater infrastructure in Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
Colby left the meeting shortly after his own remarks, before the press conference, according to two sources cited by The Telegraph, one of whom said he did not stay for Khmara’s classified briefing.
Colby “definitely appeared more on the side of Russia than on the side of Ukraine,” a German source told the publication.
Colby’s remarks follow pressure from the Trump administration on Kyiv to spare Russian refineries.
Colby also said that strikes that target “Russia’s warmaking machinery can also help contribute to slowing Russia’s advance on the front lines” and that Ukraine should not “be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back.”
Further support from European allies announced at the meeting included a pledge by Germany to buy jointly produced middle-strike and deep-strike drones, and a promise from Norway to set aside $300 million to buy Ukrainian drones, according to a Defense Ministry readout.
British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said at the same press conference that deep strikes have “helped to degrade Putin’s war machine, buying time and saving lives.” He also said Colby’s attendance in person was “a further demonstration of U.S. commitment and involvement.”
Britain’s new drones will let Ukraine target “military production facilities and other legitimate military targets far behind the front lines,” according to a government statement.
“It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” Britain’s Streeting said.

articles.title: MBDA and German startup Atmos team up to study space-based strike weapons
articles.snippet: Pan-European missile maker MBDA and German startup Atmos Space Cargo are teaming up to study deploying deep-strike weapons from Earth orbit using reentry vehicles.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — Pan-European missile maker MBDA and German startup Atmos Space Cargo are teaming up to study deploying deep-strike weapons from Earth orbit using reentry vehicles.
The firms agreed to jointly assess the feasibility and pursue development of a precision orbital deep strike capability, combining military payloads with orbital transport and reentry vehicles, they said on Wednesday. The cooperation agreement will initially focus on system architecture, technical feasibility, payload integration and possible technology demonstrations, MBDA and Atmos said.
Atmos CEO Sebastian Klaus has argued Europe needs an orbital deterrent to fill a capability gap in deep precision strike. He made the case in March for a conventional capability that can be deployed from orbit to strike any legitimate military target anywhere on Earth within 60 minutes.
“The agreement brings together our expertise in orbital transportation and atmospheric reentry with MBDA’s defense systems expertise to explore a potential new conventional defense capability,” Klaus said in a post on social network LinkedIn on Wednesday. “Our objective is clear: deterrence. To help European allies prevent aggression by strengthening the credibility of Europe’s ability to defend itself.”
The companies are assessing how existing defense technology and new orbital technology can be combined to strengthen Europe’s conventional deterrence, Klaus said in a statement on Wednesday, calling orbital transportation and return “a new layer of strategic infrastructure.”
Any future deployment and use would be subject to applicable law and decisions by the responsible governmental and military authorities, the startup said. Specific developments and future projects remain subject to further evaluation and separate agreements, according to Atmos.
Atmos will contribute expertise in orbital transportation and reentry technology, with MBDA providing capabilities in defense systems and military payloads, the companies said. MBDA, which is owned by Airbus, BAE Systems and Leonardo, is Europe’s largest missile maker.
“Our goal is to provide our armed forces with a highly innovative, sovereign European capability,” Thomas Gottschild, the managing director of MBDA Deutschland, said in a statement. “We are very much looking forward to this new project.”
Atmos is developing a reusable spacecraft for low-Earth orbit cargo missions that uses an inflatable cushion as a heat shield and aerodynamic brake for reentry. The startup successfully tested the concept in April 2025, and is developing the Phoenix 2 orbiter with a payload capacity of 100 kilograms. The company said flight duration can range from 3 hours to 12 months.
Atmos said its civilian Phoenix vehicles remain separate from the dedicated defense system being explored with MBDA.
The startup and the European Space Agency are also studying a larger version dubbed Phoenix 3 with a potential payload of about 1 metric ton.
Atmos in April this year raised €25.7 million in a Series A funding round that it said would help finance an initial three-vehicle fleet of Phoenix 2 spacecraft as well as development of Phoenix 3. The firm also said it was setting up a business serving government and defense customers called Atmos Works.
The company last year set up an alliance with ARX Robotics to integrate unmanned systems with its reentry vehicle, envisaging using Phoenix to deliver autonomous systems to the Earth’s surface, including to support defense operations on the ground.
