articles.title: DOJ, DHS partner on new unit tackling scams and cybercrime
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The departments are partnering on the Threat Disruption Center to better triage victim complaints, map cybercriminal networks and provide a direct channel to private sector organizations that work with victims.
articles.full_text:
DOJ, DHS partner on new unit tackling scams and cybercrime
The Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security announced Thursday the creation of a new task force aimed at disrupting the flow of victim funds to foreign criminal networks powering scams, cybercrime and sextortion schemes that target Americans.
The departments are partnering on the Threat Disruption Center to better triage victim complaints, map cybercriminal networks and provide a direct channel to private sector organizations that work with victims.
Senior FBI official Heith Janke said Threat Disruption Center members have already worked together on efforts to warn thousands of victims before they lose money to scammers, and the center will allow them to better coordinate their efforts.
“The Threat Disruption Center builds on those efforts by providing advanced tools and operational capabilities that enable faster action at greater scale, strengthening the work of every agency on the task force,” Janke said.
TRM Labs, which is providing technology support for the effort, said that the center has already moved to take down more than 1,600 scam websites, added more than 6,600 scam-linked cryptocurrency wallet addresses to a screening network and identified 101 new fraud networks for investigation.
The center is part of the federal government’s efforts to implement an executive order issued in March centered around stopping cyber scams, which continue to siphon billions of dollars each year from unwitting Americans.
Cyber scam losses reported to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) grew to $20.9 billion in 2025 — a number that does not account for the thousands of people who never file victim reports.
The staggering losses have prompted multiple concurrent efforts by the federal government and Congress to disrupt the scams and provide better avenues for victims to report crimes.
Much of the center's work will focus on collaborating with tech companies that get a firsthand view on criminal network activity because of how many gangs use social media platforms, web hosting, domain infrastructure, cryptocurrency services and banking systems.
“The Center establishes a standing mechanism for law enforcement and participating companies to appropriately share intelligence in near real-time, and convert that intelligence into action, for example, by pausing victim payments; taking down malicious web domains; or banning social media accounts used by scammers,” federal officials said in a statement.
“Participating private-sector companies can take these actions independently under their terms of service, while law enforcement agencies proceed with investigations, prosecutions, and court-authorized seizures.”
The center is being housed within the Homeland Security Task Force — a permanent interagency law enforcement network of more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners that focus on transnational criminal organizations, cartels and foreign terrorist organizations.
Prince Group sanctions
The initiative is just one part of a multi-prong effort the U.S. is undertaking to address cyber scams. On Thursday, for example, the Treasury Department issued more sanctions on scam operators in Myanmar and affiliates of the Prince Group, a Cambodian company accused of managing an empire of scam centers across Southeast Asia.
The sanctions include Zhao Hui, a Cambodian national who leased a scam center from Prince Group and paid the company fees to run the compound. U.S. officials accused Zhao of being directly involved in the scam center’s operations — which targeted Americans and Europeans with cryptocurrency investment scams.
Two of Hui’s companies, Bei Fang Bo Lin Construction Decoration and ZHZ Investment, are included in the sanctions.
The Treasury Department also sanctioned two leaders running the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), an armed group backing scam centers located along the Thailand-Myanmar border.
General Saw Shwe Wah is the commander-in-chief of the DKBA and Colonel Saw A One is a commander who runs the Three Pagodas Pass in Karen State near the Thai border. Both own land along the border and provide security to scam compound operators.
"These scammers rarely stop after one payment — they drain a victim's savings, or their retirement, over months and years," Esteban Castaño, CEO of TRM Labs, said of the DOJ and DHS joint venture. "Stepping in sooner changes everything: a warning before the next payment, a scam website removed before it victimizes another family, or stolen funds frozen while they can still be recovered. That's the difference between a recoverable setback and a loss from which an entire family may never recover.”
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: CISA nominee LoSapio vows to bolster cyber defenses while denying Jan. 6 Capitol attack
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency pledged to lawmakers to uncover any “gaps” within the organization while also denying the Capitol came under attack on January 6, 2021.
articles.full_text:
CISA nominee LoSapio vows to bolster cyber defenses while denying Jan. 6 Capitol attack
President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on Thursday vowed to uncover any “gaps” within the organization that have been created by massive personnel and funding cuts.
“I'm going to get involved and understand where the gaps are and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis,” Mike LoSapio, Palantir’s chief information security officer, told the Senate Homeland Security Committee.
LoSapio was nominated earlier this month to helm the nation’s cyber defense agency, which has been without a Senate-confirmed chief for almost two years. A previous nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew from consideration earlier this year after spending months in limbo on Capitol Hill. Nick Andersen has led CISA in an acting capacity since February.
The agency has been a target of Trump’s ire over the role it played in debunking the conspiracy theories he spread that the 2020 presidential election was rigged. Since he returned to the Oval Office, CISA has lost one-third of its staff and had its budget slashed by millions.
In a brief nomination hearing, LoSapio described CISA as “effectively the cybersecurity version of the 911 system. You pick up the phone, you say you have an emergency, you need help.”
“If confirmed, I intend to bring together the community and the national labs to help collaborate and coordinate and to give defenders the tools they need to defend their networks,” including AI tools, he told the panel.
In his written statement to the committee, LoSapio also pledged to “recruit and keep talented people, give them clear priorities, and make sure every dollar Congress provides is spent with discipline and tied to measurable results.”
However, he demurred when asked to weigh in on the recent technical outages that have upended key sectors of the U.S. as he’s “not inside” the agency today. And he stopped short of saying CISA’s budget needed to be increased to meet digital threats.
“I don't necessarily believe more money means more security. I believe spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk,” LoSapio told Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.).
He later testified that if analysis showed the need for more funding he would “come back to this committee and request for more resources.”
When asked by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) who won the 2020 presidential election, LoSapio repeatedly declined to directly answer.
“I'm not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” he said. “My only involvement in the 2020 election was voting for the president of the United States.”
LoSapio also disagreed with Blumenthal when the policymaker asked if the Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021.
“No, I don't believe there was an attack. No,” he said under persistent questioning.
In response, Blumenthal told LoSapio he was “disqualified from the position that you've been nominated to fill.”
The committee likely won’t vote on LoSapio’s nomination until after next week’s Thanksgiving recess. If advanced, he could face a full floor vote during the final weeks of the lame-duck session of Congress.
Martin Matishak
is the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.

articles.title: UK court confirms British government served Apple with secret encryption notice
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The British government served Apple with a secret legal notice targeting the company’s cryptographic protections for iCloud accounts, a tribunal has confirmed, ending almost two years of official refusal to acknowledge what had been widely reported.
articles.full_text:
UK court confirms British government served Apple with secret encryption notice
The British government served Apple with a secret legal notice targeting the company’s cryptographic protections for iCloud accounts, a tribunal has confirmed, ending almost two years of official refusal to acknowledge what had been widely reported.
In a judgment handed down Thursday, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal — the only court in the country that can hear certain national security cases — rejected the government’s “neither confirm nor deny” policy based on the argument that even confirming the existence of the notice would damage national security.
The court’s three judges stated explicitly that the government “has given Apple a technical capability notice,” referencing the legal power which the government used to demand that Apple retain the ability to access the content of iCloud accounts.
At the core of the dispute is Apple’s Advanced Data Protection (ADP) feature which generates and stores encryption keys on users’ own devices instead of Apple’s servers. Because Apple never holds the keys, it is technically unable to access the content of iCloud accounts even when served with a lawful request.
Last February, Apple withdrew ADP for British users entirely after receiving the technical capability notice, as was first reported by The Washington Post. Although the details of the notice are not public, it appears that Apple effectively complied by withdrawing ADP for British users.
Since the initial report about the notice, Westminster officials have continued to repeatedly state they do “not comment on operational matters, including for example confirming or denying the existence of any such notices.”
Addressing Parliament earlier this year, Security Minister Dan Jarvis again declined to respond after the issue was raised by a lawmaker, and said that not doing so was “a long-standing position held by successive Governments for obvious reasons of national security.”
Those “obvious reasons” were challenged by the tribunal, as well as in comments from both within the U.K. intelligence community and from academic experts.
In a preliminary judgment last April, the tribunal cited numerous public comments by senior U.S. politicians, including President Donald Trump, that appeared to confirm the existence of the notice, with Trump comparing the British government’s move to “something that you hear about with China.”
The then-U.S. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard ordered a legal review of the secret directive in February 2025, and said she had a “grave concern” about its implications. In its judgment, the tribunal also referenced numerous British media reports about the notice, citing government officials as sources, as additional justification for finding against the “neither confirm nor deny” policy.
Experts, including from Britain’s own intelligence community, have argued the government’s attempts to access encrypted messaging platforms should be more transparent. Academics described the Home Office's ongoing refusal to either confirm or deny the legal demand as unsustainable and unjustifiable.
Tim Stevens, the head of the King's Cyber Security Research Group at King's College London, previously told Recorded Future News that a default of no comment left the government unable to control the story when details came out.
Sir Jeremy Fleming, the former director of GCHQ, told the Munich Cyber Security Conference in 2025 that greater transparency was needed to protect the agencies’ “license to operate.”
In 2018, GCHQ technical officials argued in an essay for Lawfare that the details of any exceptional access scheme would probably become public anyway, and that criminals would not simply switch services once it was known to exist. The tribunal found that confirmation of a notice’s existence would not tell adversaries anything that they could not already find elsewhere.
Andrew Dwyer, a lecturer in information security at Royal Holloway, University of London, argued that a notice capable of removing an encryption service from millions of users is not like a live operation and should not be shielded in the same way.
The ruling does not make a finding about whether the notice issued to Apple is lawful. A substantive hearing has been scheduled for the first half of 2027.
The tribunal's April 2025 judgment, quoted again in this ruling, noted that the government can choose to withdraw or settle proceedings rather than depart from its “neither confirm nor deny” approach.
A government spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: European Commission confirms cyberattack, says hackers used AI tool
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: POLITICO had reported CERT-EU had identified the attackers’ use of ARTEX, an open-source AI hacking platform that the FBI last week warned was being used both by criminals and state-sponsored groups.
articles.full_text:
European Commission confirms cyberattack, says hackers used AI tool
The European Commission confirmed Thursday that it had been hit by a cyberattack last month involving a publicly available artificial intelligence tool, following media reports of the incident.
Speaking to journalists, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the first signs of the attack were detected October 22. He described the incident as an “AI-generated cyber campaign” but did not identify the tool used or the attackers’ apparent motivation.
POLITICO first reported that the Commission had been impacted by the cyberattack. It said CERT-EU had identified the attackers’ use of ARTEX, an open-source AI hacking platform that the FBI last week warned was being used both by criminals and state-sponsored groups.
The attack reportedly disrupted the European Commission’s personnel systems for more than 10 days, including payroll, leave requests, medical reimbursements and translation services.
A commission spokesperson confirmed to Recorded Future News they had “taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” including taking several services offline as “a protective measure.”
They said they had notified affected individuals and were “preventively checking other systems” while keeping in touch with CERT-EU and the European Data Protection Supervisor.
Regnier said investigators had found no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff broadly and were unaware of any ransom demand. He said the investigation remains open.
Asked why the incident was not disclosed earlier, Regnier said publicizing defensive measures could undermine their effectiveness. “There was no hiding whatsoever,” he told journalists.
The incident follows an alert issued in June by the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, which said AI would fundamentally transform both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities. “The timeline is not years, it is months,” it said at the time.
The FBI warned last week that ARTEX was being used prolifically by cybercriminals and nation-states to breach government agencies and dozens of critical sectors worldwide, “with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.”
The open-source framework, which was released in July, uses commercial AI models to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation.
“The key takeaway here is not that threat actors are using Artex,” said Shaun Williams, a senior director at SentinelOne, “but that the widespread availability of AI-powered tools like Artex have allowed threat actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities in internet facing devices faster, more effectively, cheaper, and with less skill than ever before.”
The attack is the Commission's third disclosed cyber incident this year, following breaches involving Ivanti software in January and its cloud infrastructure in March. Officials have not linked the incidents.

articles.title: Ukraine exposes ransomware network extorting US oil, healthcare firms
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Ukrainian authorities arrested four suspected members of an international ransomware network accused of extorting more than $40 million from companies around the world.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine exposes ransomware network extorting US oil, healthcare firms
Ukrainian authorities arrested four suspected members of an international ransomware network accused of extorting more than $40 million from companies around the world.
The operation, carried out in cooperation with the FBI, targeted a criminal organization with at least 27 members from countries including Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan, Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office said Wednesday.
Authorities linked the group, which they did not name, to a wider network of more than 60 people operating across eight jurisdictions, including former members of the notorious Conti ransomware gang. The hackers extorted at least 28 companies for a combined $40.5 million, although authorities said the total financial damage could be higher.
The hackers targeted companies in the oil and gas, pharmaceutical, manufacturing and logistics industries, as well as financial institutions and critical infrastructure operators.
During the international law enforcement operation, Ukrainian police conducted 66 coordinated searches in Kyiv and 11 other regions of the country, reportedly with the participation of U.S. law enforcement officials. Investigators seized computers, mobile phones, bank cards, about $370,000 in cash and 20,000 euros (nearly $22,000).
The four suspected key members of the organization could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Authorities said they were continuing to identify other members of the network.
Ukrainian court records reviewed by Recorded Future News identify one of the suspects as a Ukrainian citizen from the city of Dnipro. Investigators allege that he specialized in social engineering, calling employees of U.S. companies while posing as technical support staff to obtain login credentials and gain access to corporate networks. He allegedly received cryptocurrency payments for his involvement.
Alleged victims
The court documents also identify several U.S. companies allegedly targeted by the group, including oil producer Warren Oil Company, tire manufacturer Maxxis International-USA, energy services company Newpark Resources and health care services provider Quantum Health.
The hackers allegedly breached Warren Oil Company in August 2024 and stole approximately 1.4 terabytes of data. The company paid approximately $5 million in bitcoin, according to Ukrainian court records.
Two months later, the group allegedly stole 142 gigabytes of data from Maxxis International-USA. The hackers also targeted Newpark Resources in October 2024, tricking employees into revealing their credentials to gain access to the company's network. According to court records, Newpark paid $1.5 million after the attackers initially demanded $10 million.
In another attack in May and June 2026, the group allegedly demanded $15 million from Quantum Health, which ultimately paid $5 million in cryptocurrency, according to court records.
Three of the U.S. companies named in Ukrainian court records — Newpark Resources, Maxxis International-USA and Quantum Health — had previously publicly acknowledged cyberattacks, however their disclosures had not confirmed the ransom payments.
Multilayered structure
According to court records, the criminal organization had a hierarchical structure that included leaders, coordinators, social engineering specialists, technical operators and individuals responsible for handling illicit payments.
One member allegedly recruited hackers through underground forums, seeking people with expertise in programming, network administration, cybersecurity and social engineering.
The group used private communication platforms, including Rocket.Chat, qTOX and Telegram to coordinate its operations, as well as servers located outside Ukraine.
According to Ukrainian police, the hackers relied on social engineering and stolen credentials to gain access to corporate networks before deploying ransomware to pressure victims into paying. Posing as IT support employees, the attackers persuaded workers to disclose their login credentials or install remote access software, allowing them to enter corporate systems.
The attackers also developed a platform that used AI-generated voice messages to automate fraudulent phone calls, according to Maksym Tsutskiridze, acting head of Ukraine's National Police.
Once inside a company's network, the hackers stole sensitive information, encrypted files and disrupted business operations. They then demanded millions of dollars in cryptocurrency to restore access, threatening to publish the stolen data if victims refused to pay.
The court documents indicate that Ukrainian investigators obtained access to the hackers' internal communications, allowing them to reconstruct individual attacks.
The investigation also uncovered links to Conti, a once-dominant Russian-speaking ransomware operation responsible for attacks against hospitals, governments, businesses and critical infrastructure around the world. Conti effectively dissolved as an organization in 2022, but many of its members subsequently moved into other ransomware operations, including Black Basta and Royal.
Ukrainian authorities did not identify the ransomware strain used in the attacks described in Wednesday's announcement or specify which suspects had previously belonged to Conti.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
articles.snippet: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
articles.full_text:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.
Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.
“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”
Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”
“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”
Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.
One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.
Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.
“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”
Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.
“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”
How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.
The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.
“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”
Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.
Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.
Using an A/B testing platform as the delivery mechanism is a genuinely uncomfortable escalation: the tool that decides which visitors see which experience was never modeled as a malware distribution channel, so none of the usual detections fire. The operational discipline angle is what stands out – attackers versioning and measuring payloads like product features means defenders need the same rigor about what their third-party tags are allowed to change. Supply-chain reviews for marketing stacks rarely get the scrutiny payments or auth integrations do; this will change that.

articles.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.snippet: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
articles.full_text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.
The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.
The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.
Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].
Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.
The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.
IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.
Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.
The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.
Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.
Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.
A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.
That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.
More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.
Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.
Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.snippet: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.
This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.
According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.
Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.
“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”
Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.
Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.
Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).
“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”
Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.
Thank you as always. Your concern and actions for others is very much appreciated by all, including those not aware of it.

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.snippet: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”
All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.
As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

The location detail is what separates this from ordinary proxy noise: AS2650 is a fixed, well-known allocation, so any exit node registered there is either a misconfiguration worth escalating internally or an actual beacon worth watching – there’s no third reading. That Infatica nodes bundled into free apps are the vector fits the broader pattern where the resource being rented out belongs to someone who never knowingly agreed to rent it. The persistent two-week window suggests nobody at the network’s edge was watching egress, which is the cheap fix here.
